chunks: Al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr and Ṣafwān, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥajjāj, who said:
Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said to me: “Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd opposes your judges.” I said: “Yes.”

He said: “Bring me something from that over which they differed.” I said: “Two غلامs fought in the open square. One of them bit his companion, so the one who had been bitten took hold of a stone and struck with it the head of his companion who had bitten him, wounding him. Then he dealt him a blow, and he died. The matter was brought before Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, and he exacted qiṣāṣ from him. That was deemed grave by Ibn Abī Laylā and Ibn Shubrumah, and much discussion arose about it. They said: ‘This is only a mistake,’ so ʿĪsā ibn ʿAlī paid his blood-money from his own wealth.”
He said: Then he عليه السلام said: “Indeed, those with us would exact qiṣāṣ for the blow; rather, mistake is when one intends a thing but strikes something else.”

key_terms.الْمَعْضُوضُ: the one who was bitten; the assaulted party in the incident
key_terms.بِالْوَكْزَةِ: for the blow; referring to the striking act that caused death
key_terms.خَطَأٌ: mistake; an unintentional act in legal classification
key_terms.فَأَقَادَهُ: he exacted qiṣāṣ from him; he imposed retaliatory punishment
key_terms.فَوَدَاهُ: he paid blood-money for him; he compensated through diyah
key_terms.قُضَاتَكُمْ: your judges; the judicial authorities being contrasted in legal reasoning

ai.seo_question: When is a killing considered accidental rather than intentional in Islamic judicial rulings?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses a judicial case involving injury and death, and clarifies the distinction between intentional harm and accidental killing in the law of qiṣāṣ and blood-money. Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام affirms that liability for retaliation applies in such a blow, and that true mistake is when a person intends one thing but hits another.
